title: Kunun Aya
author: Ozoz Adeniyi
desc: Tiger nuts soaked overnight, blended at one part nut to two or three of water, strained through three sieves — then stood an hour or two so the starch settles and is poured off.
longDesc: Kunun aya is the tiger nut drink, and the step that separates a good one from a gritty one is the decanting. After soaking overnight, the nuts are blended repeatedly at one part nut to two or three parts water until a frothing slurry forms, flavoured with hibiscus, cardamom and alligator pepper, and strained through progressively finer sieves — three is recommended. It then stands refrigerated for one to two hours while the starch settles out, and the top liquid is decanted and the starch discarded. Most recipes omit that step, and it is the whole difference.
ingredients: Water — 1 part tiger nuts to 2-3 parts water
2 tbsp dried hibiscus flowers (flor de Jamaica)
equipment: Three sieves of progressively finer mesh, or cheesecloth
steps: Find fresh tiger nuts — preferably November or December, from street vendors.
Wash them thoroughly and remove any stones and twigs.
Soak overnight, covered by 1 to 2 inches of water.
The next day, discard the soaking liquid and rinse.
Blend at 1 part tiger nuts to 2 or 3 parts water, repeatedly, until a slurry forms and froths.
Add the hibiscus, cardamom and alligator pepper and blend again.
Pass through progressively finer sieves — three is recommended — or through cheesecloth.
Stand refrigerated 1 to 2 hours to let the starch settle.
Decant the top liquid and discard the starch.
Sweeten to taste, refrigerate, and serve within 24 to 48 hours.
chefTips: The decant is the technique. One to two hours in the fridge, then pour off the top and throw the settled starch away — this is what most recipes skip and it is why most homemade kunun aya is gritty.
Three sieves, each finer than the last. One pass through a coarse sieve will not do it.
Blend repeatedly rather than once. You are extracting, not pureeing, and it takes several passes with fresh water.
Discard the soaking water and rinse before blending. It carries the bitterness.
November and December is the fresh tiger nut season in Nigeria. Dried nuts work but need a longer soak.
Twenty-four to forty-eight hours is the window. It is an unpasteurised nut milk and it does not keep.
One part nut to two or three parts water is the stated ratio and it is the only one in the kunu family that is cleanly given.
commonMistakes: Skipping the settle-and-decant, which leaves it gritty.
Straining once through a coarse sieve.
Holding it more than two days.
sources: Adapted from 'Kunun Aya, "Horchata" de Chufas "Nigerian Style"', published on kitchenbutterfly.com, 27 November 2012. ATTRIBUTION: the byline prints as the site name; credited to the site, with Ozoz Sokoh noted as proprietor.

Quantities exactly as printed: Tiger nuts 2–3 cups; Water; Dried hibiscus flowers (Flor de Jamaica) 2 tablespoons; Cardamom pods 10–12; Alligator pepper/Grains of paradise 1 teaspoon; Sugar to taste. Blending ratio as printed: '1 part tiger nuts to 2–3 parts water'. Yield not specified.

Method as printed: locate fresh tiger nuts, preferably November/December from street vendors; wash thoroughly, remove stones and twigs; soak overnight covered by 1–2 inches of water; next day discard the soaking liquid and rinse; blend repeatedly until a slurry forms and froths; add flavourings and blend again; pass through 'progressively finer sieves (3 recommended)' or cheesecloth; 'stand refrigerated 1–2 hours to let the starch settle. Decant the top liquid, discard the starch'; sweeten to taste; refrigerate; 'serve within 24–48 hours.'
THE DECANT-AND-DISCARD-STARCH STEP IS THE TECHNIQUE POINT — it is what separates kunun aya from a gritty slurry, and most sources omit it.

BOTANY as printed: 'Cyperus esculentus var. sativus, tiger nut belongs to the plant family Cyperaceae. It is commonly known as the tiger nut, earth almond, chufa, yellow nut sedge or Zulu nuts…originally native to the Mediterranean region but its cultivation has now spread to many warm countries and has become naturalized in Ghana, Nigeria and Sierra Leone.'

THE USEFUL CORRECTION ON WHAT KUNU IS, verbatim: 'Just as Kunu refers to milky cream drinks made from cereals (millet, sorghum, rice, groundnuts), so does Horchata mean the milky extract from any vegetable source.' So kunu is a CATEGORY, not a recipe — kunun aya is one member, kunun gyada another (NGA098), kunun zaki another.
TIGER NUT NAMES ACROSS NIGERIAN LANGUAGES, as listed on the page: Hausa Arigiza or ayaa rigiza; Kanuri Sebu; Nupe Efa; Tiv Ishoho; Efik Isip akra; Igbo Akihausa; Yoruba Imumu Ofio omu or Erunsha.

FOUR KUNU VARIETIES ARE DELIBERATELY NOT PUBLISHED IN THIS COLLECTION, and the reason is a standing rule: no fermentation goes in without a documented doneness cue. KUNUN ZAKI — the most popular variety — has a well-documented germination step (3 to 4 days at 25 to 30°C, per Egwim et al.) and a steeping window of 8 to 48 hours, but its own source prints the fermentation step itself as 'Fermentation for appropriate time', giving no figure at all and no cue. KUNUN AYA IN ITS FERMENTED FORM has a time course from the MDPI typology — 'Steeping cleaned and sorted cereal and/or tiger nut seeds in water for 48–72 h' then 'Left to ferment for another 24 h' — but no doneness cue; the unfermented soak-and-blend version published above is a different preparation and carries no such risk. KUNUN TSAMIYA and KUNUN AKAMU likewise have no documented cue. NO KUNU VARIETY HAS A DOCUMENTED DONENESS CUE in anything consulted. The typology source is Ndukwe, Johnson K., Claret Chiugo Aduba, Kingsley Tochukwu Ughamba, Kenechi Onyejiaka Chukwu, Chijioke Nwoye Eze, Ogueri Nwaiwu and Helen Onyeaka, 'Diet Diversification and Priming with Kunu: An Indigenous Probiotic Cereal-Based Non-Alcoholic Beverage in Nigeria', Beverages, 2023.

A LEAD NOT RETRIEVED that would likely close those gaps: 'Nutritional composition of different types of kunu produced in Bauchi and Gombe States of Nigeria' was located on ResearchGate, which blocks automated access and was not fetched.
storage: 24 to 48 hours refrigerated, per the source. It separates and should be shaken.
healthBenefits: Tiger nut is exceptionally high in fibre and in resistant starch.
Naturally dairy-free, and a good source of magnesium and vitamin E.
Decanting the starch lowers the starch load considerably.
No added sugar unless you add it.
culturalNote: Tiger nut is the same chufa that makes Valencian horchata, and kunun aya is its Nigerian counterpart — which is a genuine culinary parallel rather than a coincidence, since the tuber travelled from the Mediterranean and naturalised across West Africa. Its names in Nigerian languages are all different, which suggests it has been around long enough for each to coin its own.
